newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - Americans upbeat on Europe car market.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Americans upbeat on Europe car market.

text.p: American car executives at the Paris Motor Show said on Tuesday they expected modest growth for the European market while European executives saw flat sales.
U.S. carmakers General Motors Corp, Ford Motor Co and Chrysler Corp were out in force and Ford Chairman Alex Trotman as well as Chrysler's Robert Eaton made personal appearances.
The U.S. companies are on a roll, bolstered by the rising yen, denting their Japanese rivals' competitive edge in the U.S. home market as well as in Europe.
They are enjoying market growth in Europe and the United States as well as explosive sales rises in Latin America,
Ford's Trotman expects 1996 European sales of some 13 to 14 million cars and a further rise by three percent in 1997.
GM Europe president Richard Donnelly told a news conference he expects a modest sales increase in western Europe this year.
"The western European car market will total about 12.65 million units in 1996, an increase of five per cent over last year, and the best market since 1992," Donnelly said.
But the Europeans were less upbeat.
PSA Peugeot Citroen chairman Jaques Calvet, also president of the ACEA European car industry association, was outright gloomy.
"As for 1997, forecasts are still very pessimistic with no expected growth," Calvet told a news conference.
"The causes are primarily related to the convergence of European economic policies designed, no matter what they say, to meet the Maastricht criteria (for a single European currency)."

Ford unveiled its minicar, the Ka, and a restyled Mondeo family car. Chrysler launched a car in a more expensive section of the market, the sleek and stylish Stratus Cabriolet 1997 which is graced by the company's new car logo.
Chrysler has decided to put the golden seal logo used by Walter P. Chrysler from 1924 back on its cars and will keep the Pentastar, which replaced it in 1962, as its corporate logo.
It is also stepping up efforts to market the Neon, made in the United States to beat Japanese competition in manufacturing simplicity in Europe.
Apart from the traditional markets, the Americans have their eyes elsewhere -- in Latin America and eastern Europe.
Ford announced a decision to built the Ka in Brazil.

"Times have changed, it used to be a market where we and other manufacturers used old products, second-hand clothes. But now Brazil needs new clothes, like any other market and we're going to put the new products in there, like the Fiesta, like the Ka and there will be others coming too," Trotman said.
Chrysler announced a $500 million joint-venture in Latin America with Bayerischen Motoren Werke (BMW) to build 400,000 small engines per year from 1999 there.
Both Chrysler's Eaton and BMW chairman Bernd Pitschetsrieder underlined the importance of the growing market in the so-called Mercosur area in Latin America.
Eastern Europe is growing fast as well and Ford's Trotman said that sales were expanding and the company was putting its structures in place there to sell more cars.
Ford Motor Credit was the first foreign issuer of a recent Polish zloty bond aimed at car financing for its Polish dealer network.
